utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. Behar is finishing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what meeting it was that you attended with Mr. Djordjevic on January 16th of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, 1999, I didn't attend the 16th of January meeting. I only drove Mr. Djordjevic, according to his request, to Mount Kopaonik on that day, and on the 17th I returned. On Mount Kopaonik we were skiing on the 17th, and during the skiing he had a telephone conversation, he told me that there were some complications in Kosovo and that he should go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm going to try and keep the questions specific if you can keep your answers specific to the question we'll move faster today. Do you know, sir, what meeting Mr. Djordjevic was attending, and do you know who was present at that meeting on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called me on the 16th to drive him there, but my police officers from the special unit provided a security detail for the government. I think the government met on the 15th and the 16th. He called me to transport him on the 16th, but my men were there providing security from the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So it sounds like there were a number of high-level government officials at this meeting or at these meetings; is that fair to say? You were providing security because there were some high-level government officials?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we provide security for these high-ranking officials. I don't know who they were because it was my men who secured these high officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And Mr. Djordjevic had come via helicopter from attending political meetings in Prizren earlier that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which means of transportation he had used. All I know is that he called me on the 16th to drive him to Kopaonik. I don't know where he had come from and whether if he flew in by helicopter. All I know is that he asked me to drive him to Mount Kopaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: He told us that he had been in Prizren and Pec in meetings, but he didn't relate that to you, or you don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that, and I honestly don't remember anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, when you saw Mr. Djordjevic on January 16th, this would have been the day after the Racak incident - we spoke about that a little bit yesterday - did you talk to Mr. Djordjevic about the Racak incident and all the publicity it was getting?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't discuss this event, nor did I know anything about the incident. He only asked me to drive him to Kopaonik for skiing, so we didn't discuss anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, surely, sir, that you would have been aware of the incident by the 16th given all the international press coverage that it was getting, international monitors were already up in arms by the 16th, William Walker had held a press conference on the 16th that was making political waves, but you maintain, sir, that neither you nor Mr. Djordjevic had heard of the Racak incident and that it never came up?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk about this incident and after all, I did not know anything about that incident. I didn't know that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were the commander of the SAJ Prishtina, Mr. Djordjevic was the chief of the public security department. Surely someone would have communicated this event, if not to you, then certainly to Mr. Djordjevic. Would you not think that would be the normal state of affairs within the ministry given something so significant for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am the commander of SAJ, but nobody informed me about the incident. As for the head of the department, I don't know whether anyone had informed him, and we never discussed the issue whether he had been informed or whether anything had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But, in fact, sir, you've already told us that Mr. Djordjevic was attending high-level meetings. We've heard from him that he was attending meetings prior to the 16th. We've heard from you as well today he was attending meetings with high-level government officials. Surely, sir, these people would have been well aware of the Racak massacre and that would have been communicated, would it not? Would that not be the normal state of affairs that you would expect for such a significant event?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know why this meeting of the government was held, and whether they discussed this incident, I truly don't know. I myself had not been informed about the Racak incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that as the chief of the department - and I ask you because in your position you would be well aware of the flow of information - would you agree with me that the chief of the department would in the normal course be kept aware of such significant events?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself. I cannot speak for the chief of department. He probably should have been informed, but I cannot make any comments on that. All I know is that I was the commander of the special unit, nobody informed me about the event, and I knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off yesterday, you had just testified quite clearly that you didn't know of any such name as the "Skorpions" during any of the time that you were with these MUP reservists. And you told us that it was only in 2002 that you first heard that name. Do you recall that discussion we had yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this yesterday. I didn't know any Skorpions. At all times there were only reservists who had been dispatched by the MUP. In all my previous statements I always referred to them as the MUP reserve forces. Perhaps I repeated myself due to the mode of questions that you asked me, but as I said, I always knew them and referred to them as the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But just to be very clear, sir, as I understood your testimony yesterday, you told us that you had never heard the name the Skorpions, and, in fact, you told us you never heard the name the Skorpions until 2002; is that correct? So just for me to be very clear, I'm not asking you what you called them, I'm asking you whether you had heard the name, the "Skorpions" associated with those men prior to 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that name. I didn't know that they were called Skorpions. In 1999 when they came to us, they were members of the MUP reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let's look at that. But I want to first ask you, what was the size of your regular unit in 1999? I want to make sure I have this right. I believe you said there were about 100 people in the SAJ Prishtina and about the same in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that according to the job classification for the unit, it numbered 100 men. However, 50 to 60 of them were able to take part in the tasks that we performed. When I said 100 men, I meant that it was a unit composed of several platoons, the 1st one, the 2nd one, and the 3rd one, and the 3rd Platoon had hygiene workers, logistical section, mechanics, drivers, et cetera. So the part of the unit that was directly involved in tasks was not 100 but rather 50 to 60, which equals approximately two platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And these Skorpions or this MUP reserve unit, as you referred to it, that numbered about 128 men; correct? And I'm talking about now when they were deployed with you.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reserve force numbered approximately 128 men, the first time they came as reservists. I think it's 128, maybe my memory doesn't serve me too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You are saying the first time, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 128 of them came on the 28th of March, 1999, and we sent them back from Kosovo and Metohija in 1999 after the crime that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And how do you know it was 128?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that by Commander Trajkovic on the day when Tutinac was supposed to go and bring them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And when these men were redeployed with you, how many would that be when they were reattached to the SAJ? Was it the same number?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our commander Trajkovic when this reserve force was introduced for the second time, or rather, brought to Kosovo Polje, were deployed with Mr. Simovic and myself. He divided this group of men, and he guaranteed that they would be fully screened in comparison to the 128 who had committed the crime and that as a result, there would be fewer of them, and I think the number of the people who came to Kosovo Polje was lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, we can get to that, sir. But what I want to ask you about at this point is that you have 128 men initially coming to join you, you're saying less, but certainly a significant number by any account who are redeployed with you. Now, sir, with this number of men coming to join your unit, when you only had 50 or 60 men operationally active at that time, that would radically affect your command role, would it not? You would suddenly be responsible for a significant number of additional men. It would, in fact, completely change the nature of your command; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came first time round, they did not join my unit on the 28th and were actually sent back immediately after the crime had been committed. I was, after that, in command of my men who were members of my special unit when these reservists were returned to Prolom Banja on 28th and they had not actually been attached to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But, sir, if you can just focus on my question. I know it was the intention, I think everyone has been clear about that, it was the intention for these men at the outset to be joined with your unit, and then later, I think it's clear by all accounts they were joined and they joined you in the field. So my question is, sir, adding all of these men to your command would significantly change your role as commander, would it not? You would suddenly be responsible for a significant additional number of men; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when they join us for the second time, I'm talking about the reserve forces in Kosovo, but they did not significantly change any command structure. I had been trained as an officer and, therefore, there was no problem for me to lead 100 strong company. As the reserve forces, they were mainly involved in providing security and they were not involved in operational tasks carried out by members of the SAJ that I was in command of and that I led.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that, sir, because in order to properly command these men, the significant additional number of men, you would have to have been told about who they were, where they had come from, and in particular what experience they had; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were attached to my unit for the second time, they carried out these tasks. After Commander Trajkovic assigned these men to me, I asked and inquired about their specialties and according to that, I assigned tasks to them. Some of them were sent to provide security for our facilities, and some of them were securing the lines reached. So it was possible to keep them under control. There was no need for any significant expertise on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But my point is, sir, that you would need to have been told from the outset what kind of men you were getting, what they were capable of, what their experience was, and surely this would have been communicated to you from the outset by the people who had decided that these men would be sent to you in the first place. You agree?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were admitted to the reserve forces after finishing the military service. Based on that, we made inquiries, and based on that we assigned tasks to them. That's why I said that for the most part they were used to secure facilities and the lines reached during our actions in order to give an opportunity for the active duty members of the SAJ to have some rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, if you were going to send a platoon to complete a certain task let's say to capture a hill, to secure a town, or secure certain facilities that might come under fire, you would certainly need to know if they were capable of doing that; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that our men were trained to capture any hills or elevations, and after doing that by my police officers, that is to say, the SAJ police officers, these other men provided security. They never joined me in the actions leading to the capturing of any elevations. As I said, they provided security for these features that we had captured in order for our men to have some rest. They did not take part in the seisure of any features.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, it sounds, perhaps, sir, that it was communicated to you that these men did not have much operational training or expertise or many skills. Was that, in fact, communicated to you from the outset, and was it communicated to you that because of that, because of that lack of skills, that they would have to play the secondary role? Was that understood from the outset?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that special anti-terrorist unit was an elite unit and that this reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia were not sent down there as an elite force, but rather as a reserve force precisely for the purpose of providing security of our positions and the unit while they are resting. They were securing the features during those periods. So these forces that were attached to us were reserve forces, and I didn't know what skills they possessed. But we didn't need any special skills. We only needed them for providing security of the lines reached and for guard duties, so they didn't need any special experience in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see the evidence of the 19th of April at T-13606, please. And I'll need line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So if we look at line 22 here, sir, Mr. Simovic was very clear in his testimony that Mr. Trajkovic told him directly that these were the Skorpions, even before they were admitted to the MUP reserve force. I want to show that to you, sir. If we look at line 22 here, and, sir, I'll just read it to you so you receive the translation. He was asked: "So it seems to me that you are saying that Mr. Trajkovic told you that they were called the Skorpions?" And he answered: "I said that I heard that from my conversation with Trajkovic, even before they had been admitted to the reserve forces. Up until that time, I didn't know that." So surely, sir, if this was communicated so readily to Mr. Simovic with this number of new men coming under your command, men you would have to know and lead in the field, you would also have been told who they were and where they were from. So were you not, sir, at this early stage before they were even put into the MUP reserve told that these men were the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not heard anything about the Skorpions. I knew them as the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia. And around the time of their admission, what Simovic said, how Simovic knew, I know that they were reserve forces of the MUP and that some of them had been admitted into this reserve force of the MUP in 1999 by the administration of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So do you still deny, sir, that you had heard the name the Skorpions prior to 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I heard the name Skorpions before 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the uniform that you normally wore in the SAJ? And I know you did, in fact, have several uniforms. Perhaps you can describe the uniform that you were wearing in the field in 1999.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I wore, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Did you wear the same uniform as your men?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, I did wear the uniform of my active duty servicemen. The NATO camouflage uniform which has a green-brown patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: What about the patch on your sleeve, sir, can you describe what that would look like?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our insignia. We had insignia of the SAJ on the cap and a patch on the sleeve with the lettering S-A-J. It's the same one worn by the SAJ today. That is what we wore in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Is this the patch that has the emblem of the double-headed eagle with a red shield and the Serb symbol with the four Cs or Ss?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this emblem is on the sleeve. I don't remember whether it was the left or the right sleeve at the time. It's a double-headed eagle. There is a sword and a snake, I think. It's grey in colour, metallic grey, and I'm not sure about the four letter Cs or Ss, but I'm sure about the sword. We had also another insignia worn on the ceremonial type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the colour is not grey there, it's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we've learned, we've heard in this trial already about the uniforms that were worn by these new volunteers, these MUP reservists. In particular, we heard about the special patch that they wore on their other shoulder. Can you describe that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these reservists of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in the regular police uniform of the reserve force with the insignia of the ministry. I didn't see any other emblem or insignia on these reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, that's not what we've heard, sir. We've heard that they were issued the NATO camouflage pattern of uniforms, and what we've heard is that they wore the SAJ patch or insignia on one arm and on the other arm they wore a Skorpions patch. I'll take you through that. What we've heard, sir, is this was a patch that had a Skorpion on it. Are you familiar with that? Surely you would recall seeing that.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that. The emblem of the SAJ could be worn only by a member of the SAJ, certainly not the reserve force, and I maintain that because nobody would have been able to wear that emblem of the SAJ without being a member, not the reserve force certainly. The emblem of the SAJ was worn only by the active duty servicemen in the special anti-terrorist unit of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's look, then, at P493. And we'll need page 7 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, this is the statement again of Mr. Stoparic, we've looked at that before. I want to show you what a member of the Skorpions himself has described. If we look at paragraph 40, it's just on the bottom of your page, sir, it's in middle in English. And I'll just read you one phrase from here just to situate what he is talking about. He says, sir, towards the bottom of that paragraph: "Altogether there were around 120 men or volunteers in total. We all had been told not to bring any of our former or personal military equipment with us as we would be issued with uniforms and weapons before going to Kosovo." What I really want to show you, sir, is on the next page in the B/C/S, and just underneath in English. If we look at the second line in paragraph 41, sir, he says: "It was dark by the time we arrived. Here in the field were policemen in uniform at desks with piles of uniforms." And if I just move ahead a little bit he says: "Here we were all issued with two sets of uniform, a combat vest, matches, gloves, boots, et cetera." So I just want to go step by step here, sir. Mr. Stoparic describes that these uniforms were already prepared and they were there waiting for them, and they were issued by uniformed police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I don't remember this. I don't know what Mr. Stoparic said. I'm saying what I know. The reserve force of the MUP when they came to us had the regular uniform of the Ministry of Interior, and I really, really never saw them with this kind of uniform. I don't know what they were issued with. It's true that probably the ministry issued them with uniforms, but the uniform of the reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior. I don't know what this gentleman was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the first line of paragraph 42 he says very clearly: "The uniforms were of NATO colour and pattern ," just as you've described the normal issue for the SAJ. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. I see what is written in that line, but the SAJ always had uniforms of this colour plus another uniform. Stoparic could have described it because he knew it, but I really never saw them wearing that uniform normally worn by the SAJ of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, this is really what I want to show you, if we could go back to paragraph 41 right after where I had -- the spot where I had left off when I was reading from there earlier. He says: "We had both the SAJ patch insignia," that's the sword with the four S, the Serbian S. "We had both the SAJ patch insignia and the Skorpion patch insignia, one for each arm of the uniform." So do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it written. What I'm saying is that this reserve force was dressed in regular police uniforms, that they did not have the kind of SAJ insignia that I was wearing because they were reservists and they could not wear that insignia. They wore the regular insignia of the MUP. The emblem of the SAJ could be worn only by an active-duty police officer who was a member of the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, if special SAJ uniforms were already there waiting for these men that had been customized with Skorpion patches on the shoulder, then the fact that these were Skorpions, that these men called themselves the Skorpions would have been well known within the ministry; correct? In other words, someone had taken the time and effort and forethought to have these uniforms with the Skorpions patch there waiting for these men?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I claim with full responsibility that this was the reserve force of the MUP. SAJ uniforms were issued only to us. I had them, Simovic had them as the commander, and we had our own depots where uniforms were issued exclusively to our employees. Certainly not to the reserve force. The reserve force was equipped by the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, when you were out in the field we've heard that you would use radios to communicate with each other and you would communicate use call-signs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used signs, not codes in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Names that would be used as a call-sign, and sometimes we designated secret call-signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see paragraph 69, please. It's on page 12. Perhaps we can just zoom in a little bit on paragraph 69 on both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Stoparic also spoke about communication in the field, and if you look at the middle of this paragraph 69, it's -- I believe it's the third line in. He states: "The platoon and unit commanders were equipped with Motorola radios for communication. We used the old Skorpion call-signs, 'Skorpion 1,' 'Skorpion 2,' et cetera." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So these platoons, sir, these Skorpion platoons, were even referring to themselves over the radio in communications as Skorpions, Skorpion 1, Skorpion 2. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that they were Skorpion 1, Skorpion 2, et cetera. They were attached to us so they couldn't have these names Skorpion 1 or Skorpion 2. They were attached, seconded to us, and they were working together with our active-duty force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, your men were paid per diems; correct? You understand what I mean by that? Certain occasions you would be paid a -- your men would be paid a daily amount, a per diem?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We did receive per diem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: As a commander, is that something that you would have to oversee or sign off on?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed for my active duty force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You would have to confirm who was present and who would get paid; is that right? So who would receive a per diem for certain days being present?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I signed off I had to make sure exactly who I was signing for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: What about expenses, sir, if expenses were incurred and then needed to be reimbursed by the ministry, is that something that would also go through you, that you would have to sign off on?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What kind of expenses do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Were there occasions, sir, where maybe certain unusual expenses had to be taken or paid in the field that then would need to be submitted to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mainly the commander who signed off on those lists and expenses as well. We would send it to the commander for him to sign and then it would go on to further processing in the services of the Ministry of Interior. The joint services. Receipts for food or per diem or whatever receipts would be forwarded to the services who took care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see the transcript from this trial from the 28th of September, 2009 at T-9099, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I want to show you what your commander, Mr. Trajkovic, said. I'll read it again to you so you receive the translation. This is at line 13. He said: "Even in our lists for the payment of per diems and other expenses, due to Mr. Slobodan Medic that group came to be known as the Skorpions." So, sir, it would appear that even for something as official within the ministry as a payment for per diems or other expenses, these men were known as the Skorpions. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Trajkovic said. I only know that per diem and all the other expenses were settled by specific names, by specific individuals. No one was ever paid on the basis of a nickname, just the full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, these men, these Skorpions or MUP reservists, they were known to be from Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. That was a known hotbed for paramilitaries, was it not? In fact, a number of paramilitaries were known to operate in that area?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a reserve force of the MUP. A reserve force of the MUP. I did not know them as Skorpions, I mean, and they also had been in that region where Zivko Trajkovic first met them, when Zivko was staying in that area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I don't know how Zivko was there, but I know he was staying in that area at some point, and I know he first met them in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't answer my question and I need you to focus on my question and answer my question. My question for you is, that area, this area of Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem where you knew these men were from, that area was known to be an area where there was significant paramilitary activity; correct? In other words, it was commonly known, it would have been commonly known to you and to others that there were a number of paramilitary groups operating there. Is that something you knew?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was a commander of the special unit in Prishtina, and I did not know what existed or had existed in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, I had never been in that area so I really don't know if there had been paramilitary formations or not. I've never been to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, nor do I know that there had been paramilitary units in the sense that you are asking me now in this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, everyone knew, including yourself, that these men were commanded by and associated with Slobodan Medic. Was it not notorious, was it not very well known that Mr. Medic led the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Medic arrived then as a MUP reservist, I knew him as a simple reservist. I don't know what Boca had been. That day when he came, he just introduced himself to me as Boca. No mention of commander, no mention of Skorpions. That's all I know at the moment he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I want to take a moment, if we can, we can put aside some of your other knowledge, and I want to just look at the name, this name, the Skorpions. Would you agree with me, sir, that the fact that a unit would call itself the Skorpions would convey immediately to anyone who knew that they were calling themselves the Skorpions that this wasn't a regular group of professional policemen or soldiers. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this before. I really didn't know them. To me it was the reserve force of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. They had been admitted to the reserve force of the MUP. I didn't know who they had been earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's not repeat that, you've gone over and over that same line. Let me put it this way then, sir: If you had known at any time that a group called itself the Skorpions, a group of men called themselves the Skorpions, would that not itself indicate to you that this was not an ordinary group of professionals or an ordinary group of men if they had all chosen to go by the name the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm repeating again, I did not know. It was just the reserve force, and I didn't know that they were calling themselves Skorpions. For that reason, I knew only that they were the reserve force of the MUP, nothing else was known to me on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you are still not answering my question, so let me put it as bluntly as I can. If someone approached you and said to you, we have a group of men that call themselves the Skorpions, we want to put them into your unit under your command, would that indicate a problem to you, sir, with respect to who these men were and what their background was?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I understand the question better. Regardless, I mean, if I now learned of the existence of a group, the kind you are mentioning now, Skorpions or something like that, of course that would set me thinking how somebody who is supposed to be the reserve force of the MUP and is calling themselves by another name, that would certainly make me question what kind of unit that was, but they had arrived as a reserve force of the MUP, and I never heard them calling themselves the Skorpions. I'm claiming that with full responsibility as the then-commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I want to look very quickly, if I can, at the names of some of the other very well known militia group, each of which, I think you'll be able to see has a similar nickname. Surely, sir, you are familiar with the Tigers, Arkan's Tigers? You've heard of them?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of them after the wars in Bosnia and Slavonia, yes, I did hear of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, they fought across Eastern Slavonia, the same area where the Skorpions originated; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they had been fighting, but I heard of Arkan's Tigers, and I really don't know where they were involved in combat. I was commander in Kosovo, and if you look at Kosovo and Slavonia, they are very far away from one another, and I don't know where the Tigers had been fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, Arkan was quite notorious, I know even for those of us who lived far away from Serbia, many of us had heard of him. I'm surprised you didn't know more about this man. Let me ask you this, sir, were you aware that Arkan was indicted by this Tribunal on September 30th of 1997, that would be a year and a half before the Skorpions were attached to your unit? Were you aware, sir, that Arkan was indicted by this Tribunal in 1997?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that this Tribunal indicted Arkan. I heard of him in the same manner that I heard of his Tigers. As for your question involving the information about the indictment, why would I be required to know when the indictment against Arkan was issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the White Eagles, sir? Have you heard of that group, also known as the Avengers?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard of this kind of group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: How about the Yellow Wasps, sir, have you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of Yellow Wasps either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That surprises me, sir, because the leader of the Yellow Wasp, Vojin Vukicevic was arrested in Belgrade in a joint action of the SAJ and the state security service. Surely you would have been aware of that as a member and, in fact, a commander of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was the commander of the Prishtina SAJ. I've never heard of this action. This is the first time that I hear it from you. I would just like to underline once again that I was a commander of SAJ Pristina. I wasn't the commander of the SAJ Belgrade or the SAJ of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, such a notorious fact as the arrest by the SAJ of a paramilitary leader, that wouldn't be known to you as the commander of the SAJ Pristina even if it was done by the SAJ Belgrade under Mr. Simovic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, with regard to this, I'm telling you that I hadn't heard of this. I was in command of the Pristina SAJ, and I knew as much as I needed to know. I was in charge and in command of my unit. I don't know about the arrest, who did the arrest, and I claim with full responsibility that I didn't know anything about what you are asking me, and I still don't know anything to this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not regret -- react when this line of questioning was initiated, although some of them have to do with the topic that we are discussing today. However, I think that this is now going beyond certain knowledge that this witness might have especially with regard to the questions about the arrest and other things. I think that this is a much too broad subject for this witness to be able to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly this line of questioning is not about the precise facts of this case. It does appear to be directed to credit. At least for the present, the Chamber won't interfere. Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Yes, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I am -- we will move off this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I just have one general question for you, sir, just to wrap all of this up. Surely, sir, with the well known recent history of these paramilitaries that were operating throughout the former Yugoslavia, as a professional soldier, you would need to be extremely careful about the dangers that those type of paramilitaries might pose; is that correct, sir? Do you agree that given that history anyone ought to have been aware of and concerned with the role of paramilitaries within the military structure and the police structure?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this question is concerned, I was in command of a special anti-terrorist unit of the Ministry of the Interior. This unit never had volunteer units, nor did it have reserve force, nor any paramilitary formations. I exclusively worked with police officers who were professional servicemen. The first time we had some kind of reserve force was after the minister decided to engage these reserve forces that were subsequently attached to us in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see P493 once again. If we can look at page 3, paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just going back quickly to the statement of Mr. Stoparic, sir, and there's a specific question I want to ask you about this. If we look at paragraph 11. Sir, Mr. Stoparic described here that the Skorpions unit was, in fact, on the payroll of the RDB when they were in Eastern Slavonia, so this would have been in the early 1990s. I wanted to give you a chance to see that. You can read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I see my friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the translation that we received came from the RDB, and I think that is what the transcript reflects. I think the document says something completely different. I'm not sure whether my learned friend, Mr. Behar, read it carefully because there is a discrepancy between the transcript and the translation, so could he kindly repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the discrepancy is my friend is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can proceed, sir, but what I wanted to ask you is if someone had been on the payroll of the ministry, then would information about who those men were be readily available to personnel within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about these persons being on the payroll of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: What I want to ask you, sir, is if they were on the payroll, and I understand you may not have known that, if they were on the payroll, sir, does that not mean that that information, that the information that was known about them would be easily available to someone within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm asserting again that they were on the payroll for the daily allowance payments when they were with me. I'm talking solely about the reserve forces that were attached to my unit, and we made this kind of list. This is the first time that I see this, and I know nothing about what it reads. I'm telling you again that I was engaged in Kosovo with the special anti-terrorist unit of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, and I honestly don't know anything about what you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that the Skorpions were involved in committing murders in Trnovo, Bosnia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, during a trial that took place and about which I read in the papers and heard on the media, I heard something about them having committed a crime in Trnovo in Bosnia if I'm not mistaken. Somewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that Slobodan Medic who you've described meeting and interacting with, was convicted and sentenced for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I knew Medic then as Boca. I later learned from the media that some people were convicted for this crime. Whether Slobodan Medic was amongst them, I can't remember now. I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, I might have thought that a man that you knew and had worked with going to jail, being convicted and sentenced for such a notorious high-profile crime is something that you would remember quite well. Are you saying that you are not even sure if that had happened? You don't recollect that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that any of them had committed any crime at the time when they came as the reserve force, and I'm repeating again that about this crime and about what had happened in Trnovo, I learned through the media, or rather, I was watching it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let's get back to the events in Podujevo on the 28th of March. We've spoken a lot about all of the effort that was taken to assemble these reservists, to arm them, to uniform them. Sir, what I want to ask you is after -- from the time that they were sent into Podujevo, how long were they on the ground before this massacre was committed?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat. I didn't understand the question fully. From the moment when they came to Podujevo until the time when the crime was committed? Well, they arrived on the 28th of March in Podujevo sometime in the morning. From the moment when Simovic and Boca came to my office at the staff headquarters, about 30 or 40 minutes elapsed before we heard the shots. So not long after they came to my office is when that happened, but I cannot be quite sure and tell exactly whether it was half an hour or 40 minutes or something, but it was shortly after they arrived in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a very simple question. Did you attend the scene of the killings after that massacre had taken place?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't visit the scene. The commander of the Belgrade SAJ Tutinac, Zoran Simovic, were there as well as Dr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you were the commander of the Pristina SAJ. You heard shots ringing out, you knew people were wounded because the doctor was there, I think on all accounts the doctor was there, whether you dispatched him or not, and so one would think either some civilians had been killed given that firing and given the injuries, the wounding. Either that or there's a battle going on, and I would suggest to you that either way, sir, this is going to be very important for the commander to know. You needed to know what was going on there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I was in the staff HQ, and an officer should remain there. Immediately after the shooting, Mr. Simovic and the doctor, Dr. Markovic, went to the crime scene, and I, as an officer, as soon as I heard that there were people wounded, I provided a vehicle and a driver and made arrangements for them to be transported to a hospital in Pristina. I'm talking about the people who were wounded or injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But, is it your testimony, sir, that you never attending the scene? At no point when you were in Podujevo did you go to that scene where that massacre had taken place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to the scene. Commander Simovic was there. I was at the command, and I notified the duty officer at the Podujevo OUP and instructed him to organise and arrange for an on-site investigation, to cordon off the area, and to carry out all the procedures, standard procedures that should be done in such instances. I was at the Podujevo OUP premises, and I didn't visit the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So, you just stayed inside this room during the entire events that took place? You heard a massacre had been committed, there were all sorts of people on the scene, it may have been committed by these Skorpions, and you just stayed in the room the whole time?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there until the notification was sent out and Simovic went to the scene. After that, I did not go to visit the crime scene. I didn't go there. Mr. Simovic, Zoran, Zoran Simovic was on the spot. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, as the commander of the SAJ Pristina what steps did you take to ensure that a full and proper investigation into that massacre was conducted?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander of Pristina SAJ, I notified the police officer at the Podujevo OUP about the incident that took place in Podujevo. The officer in charge at the OUP Podujevo was duty-bound to arrange for an investigating judge and a prosecutor to go to the crime scene and to carry out all the proper procedures in order to establish how many casualties were as a result of the crime that took place on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Is that all you did, sir? You just informed the Podujevo OUP that something had happened?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed the OUP Podujevo not that something had happened, but that a crime had been committed, that civilians had been killed. The officer in charge at the OUP Podujevo was duty-bound to inform the prosecutor and other people who were obliged to carry out an on-site investigation. Once I did what I was supposed to do that as a uniformed official, it was up to them to visit the crime scene and to establish what exactly happened on that day in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you testified yesterday that you lined up your men and the men from the SAJ Belgrade and asked them if they committed the crime or if they had scene the perpetrators. Do you recall saying that yesterday? I can give my friend the reference. It's T-13786, line 19.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I noticed when I asked you what steps you took, sir, just a moment ago, you didn't mention that. Did you, in fact, do that, sir? Did you, in fact, line up your men and the men from SAJ Belgrade and ask them if they committed the crime or saw the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Prosecutor. That's what I said yesterday. I did that after we sent those men back to Prolom Banja. The men from SAJ Pristina and SAJ Belgrade remained there. I lined them up, and I asked them if it was someone among them who committed the crime or if they had seen the perpetrators. They told me that they didn't. I ordered the platoon commanders to check with all our men from both units whether all the weapons and the ammunitions were in place after they carried out these checks. They said that everything was accounted for and in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll get to that as well, sir. My question for you, sir, is why did the now line up the Skorpions or those MUP reservists and ask them? Would that not have been the smarter thing to do, and, in fact, the obvious thing to do?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to the crime scene. It was Mr. Zoran Simovic who went there. I was at the command HQ, which is not far away. After the reserve force had been sent back, I did this with the active-duty personnel of both SAJ units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Would you have lined them up and asked them those questions, sir, if that Skorpion unit was still in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe, but these combat operations were in progress and they came by buses. There was danger involved, and there was a group of people, but I truly cannot tell you what I would have done. I wasn't there. I don't know whether I would have lined them up or not. All I'm telling you is what I did with the active-duty personnel of both SAJ units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Is it good police practice, sir, to take the prime suspects for a serious crime and remove them from the scene?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent back to the Podujevo OUP. We supposed that it was them who committed the crime. However, since the bombing was constantly in progress, we couldn't establish that at the moment. They asked the men from the reserve force, but we were unable to establish who the perpetrators was, then we sent them back to Prolom Banja. It was Zoran who escorted them to Prolom Banja on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that it was the bombing that prevented you from being able to establish or even look into who had committed this crime? This is the first we've heard of that. Are you saying it was the NATO bombing that prevented any investigation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps -- well, you know, we organised for an on-site investigation to be carried out by an investigating judge at the scene of crime. It wasn't the bombing that prevented us from doing that, but I as commander of a special unit of Pristina or my men who were there, we were not trained in carrying out crime scene investigations to find out who the perpetrators were, et cetera. We were simply -- I was not simply trained to do that. That is why we notified the regional police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's sufficient, sir. But surely, you had enough police training to know that it was not good police practice to send the prime suspects for a crime away from the crime scene and, in fact, away from the Podujevo OUP police who would be doing the investigation? Would you not agree with that, sir? Good police practice does not involve sending the suspects away from the scene and away from the investigators?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our estimate at that moment that an on-site investigation should be done in Podujevo where the crime happened, and that the best thing to do at that memo was to send back that reserve force because there was the NATO bombing, we thought the best thing to do was to return them to the place where we had collected them from, namely Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, what steps did you take to make sure that those men would be held and questioned in Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take any steps. We sent them back. I did not do that, but the regional secretariats were supposed to do that at the place where the men were sent. In this case, the secretariat in Prokuplje which has territorial jurisdiction over Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Did you secure the crime scene, sir, where all those women and children had been shot?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did pending the arrival of this team from OUP Podujevo and the commanding officer who was supposed to organise the investigation on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And what did you do, sir? You specifically. What steps did you take to secure the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when it happened, I've already said I informed the police administration in OUP Podujevo, and the personnel who happened to be at the crime scene at the time of the crime remained to secure the scene until OUP Podujevo officers arrived to conduct a crime scene investigation. I was still at the headquarters of the OUP Podujevo, not far from the building where it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Then it would seem that you wouldn't know that, sir, that any steps had been taken to secure the crime scene if you were never at the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the men who were there on the spot, our employees, who were giving first aid to the injured along with the doctor, they were on the scene, and they just stayed there as guards pending the arrival from their commanding officer of the OUP Podujevo and the other team for crime scene investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I see we are at the time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just before the break, one small request. Line 22, page 29, I think it reads that they were returned to Podujevo instead of Prolom Banja, and that's the only correction I wanted to make before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that was the only difficulty with our transcript, our life would be quite easy, wouldn't it? Thank you. We will have the first break now. Your time estimation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll be done in the next session, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole of the next session?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. Possibly half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Think about a quarter of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off just before the break you told us about how the Skorpions or this MUP reserve unit was sent back to Prolom Banja right after the massacre was committed. And we know as well from your testimony, in that of Mr. Simovic, that several weeks later these men were redeployed and attached to the SAJ, and they had joined your unit in the field. My question for you, sir, is: When did you first learn that this was going to happen, that these men would be reattached and would join you in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the commander arrived, I mean Commander Trajkovic, he told us that we were to get a reserve force again at one of the regular meetings he had with me and Simovic he told us that, in the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Do you remember when in the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was sometime in April when he said we were about to get a reserve force and that reserve force of the MUP indeed arrived towards the end of April when we were going into one of the actions together with them. I believe it was in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So you said earlier it was the beginning of April. Bearing in mind that it was the 28th of March that these men were involved in the incident and then sent back, would you say it was -- I'm talking now about the time you spoke to Mr. Trajkovic. Would you say that it was a period of one week after March 28th or two weeks after March 28th when Mr. Trajkovic told you this?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly a week, that's seven days, right. I can't say exactly when we had this talk, but I know we had this talk. I know that Simovic was there as well. Ten, 15 days it could have been. I can't tell you exactly how many days elapsed from the moment when we sent them back until the moment when Zivko Trajkovic told us we would get a reserve force again. Around 10, 15 days maybe. But I'm sure that they were attached to us for an action in the second half of April 1999 when Trajkovic brought them to Kosovo Polje and attached one part of them to me and another part of them to Mr. Simovic from the SAJ of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So if I'm understanding right, there was a time gap between when Mr. Trajkovic told you that they were going to be reattached and then when the men actually showed up and rejoined you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was a time gap from the moment when he told us until the moment when the reserve force arrived. Not as soon as he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So Mr. Simovic had sent these men away from the scene in Podujevo because they had murdered women and children, and then they are sent almost immediately right back to you and put under your command. Were you concerned, sir, that this group of men who it appears had murdered women and children within 20 or 30 minutes of being deployed, were you concerned that they might do something like that again?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, when we were told that this reserve force of the MUP was coming, Commander Trajkovic said he was the guarantor for this reserve force, that they would honestly and honourably carry out the tasks given to them. I had no doubts about the decision of my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: What was your reaction, sir, when you first found out that these men would be rejoining you after what they had done? Your personal reaction.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Trajkovic said this reserve force was coming and that he gave his own guarantees, that set me thinking, but still, if the commander said he was the guarantor and that they would honestly and honourably carry out their tasks, I really had no reason to doubt my own commander Zivko Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Trajkovic tell you the basis for that guarantee? How could he know that nothing would happen after such a terrible massacre happened so soon after their first deployment?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he guaranteed for them as members of the reserve force. Once they are re-engaged under his own command, he guaranteed that they would not do anything again or create an incident. He even knew some of those men from before, from the time when he had been in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and that's probably why he was able to guarantee that they would work quite professionally under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what Mr. Simovic's reaction was when he found this out? Mr. Simovic is the man, it seems, who ordered these men out of Podujevo, sent them away, now they are being sent right back to him. What was his reaction when he was told this, that he was getting them back?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the same feeling, both of us. It wasn't quite all the same. We were not indifferent to the fact that the people who had committed these crimes were reservists. But after we sent them back and they came around the second time, Trajkovic said at that meeting that this force would be purged and screened and there would not be among them any men who had been responsible for any incidents, that he personally guaranteed for their work and conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, you are mentioning that now, sir, but you hadn't mentioned that before, this suggestion that the force would be purged and screened. Do you recall that when I asked you what was the basis for his guarantee, sir, you didn't say anything about the fact that different members might be joining you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I certainly mentioned it yesterday in my evidence. I said that Commander Trajkovic told me and Simovic at that meeting that these would be men who were part of a purged force, that they would not do anything again, and that he gave his guarantees. I said that yesterday, and I'm telling you again today that Commander Trajkovic told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But, in fact, sir, the only man who was removed from that force who was thought to be potentially involved in the massacre was Sasa Cvjetan; correct? The rest of the men returned?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. I don't know who was involved in that massacre. And at that time I didn't know at all, and I don't know that Sasa Cvjetan had been removed from that force when they arrived again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, to have these men be sent back to you after you had already sent them away after Mr. Simovic had sent them away, that order to reattach them to your unit must have come from high up; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simovic and I could not decide about their engagement. However, at the request of our commander that was approved again to reintroduce them into the reserve force of the MUP and to attach them to our units in Kosovo Polje in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've told us that your commander made the request. Who approved it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to requests made by our commander, or applications, all the requests concerning us in Kosovo were made by us to our commander and that was forwarded then to the MUP staff for combat against terrorism in the province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I know you keep repeating that, sir, but, in fact, the approval of the chief of the department, Mr. Djordjevic, was also required and was also given for the redeployment of those reservists; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said the decision to admit someone into the reserve force is made by the minister. The police administration in the MUP admits men into the reserve force. That is handled by the police administration, and after this procedure is completed, the procedure of admission, notification is issued about the formation of the reserve force pursuant to the decision of the minister on the constitution of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, you don't seem to be answering my question. I asked you about Mr. Djordjevic, the chief of the department. And I asked you whether his approval was required and whether it was given for the redeployment of those reservists. Dealing just with Mr. Djordjevic, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it went, but the procedure should have been as follows: My commander Zivko Trajkovic was supposed to send notifications about the needs for reservists to the chief of the department, and the chief of the department should then handle this request, and then the police administration was supposed to carry out that procedure to be decided by the minister. The decision is, therefore, made by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So, in fact, it was the chief of the department, sir, who Mr. Trajkovic had to report to, it was the chief of the department who would handle the request; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he certainly asked the department chief at that time in 1999 when the MUP staff was formed, when admissions into the force were required, approval had to be awaited from the minister about the admission. The minister made the decision, but he was supposed to inform the chief of the department about admissions. He should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see D442, please. If we can have page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report written from your commander, Mr. Trajkovic, to the chief of the department, Mr. Djordjevic. And if you just look at the last paragraph, and in English we'll look at the second last paragraph. I can just read this to you. Mr. Trajkovic explains here to

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: "A need again arose for the engagement of reservists so at the proposal of the SAJ commander, Zivko Trajkovic, and with the approval of the staff in Pristina and the chief of the department, 108 reservists were engaged under the leadership of Slobodan Medic." You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the beginning of the sentence, the need again arose for the engagement of reservists. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll just let you read that to yourself, sir. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you can see that according to your commander, Mr. Trajkovic, and he is communicating this to General Djordjevic, General Djordjevic gave his approval as required. Is that in accordance with the standard procedure you just described?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw what is written, but it says, in the part we removed now, that Trajkovic informed the MUP staff in Pristina, because I no longer see the beginning of the sentence now, and he was required to do that because he was himself a member of the staff. And "and the chief of the department, 180 [as interpreted] members of the reserve staff were engaged, led by" I don't know what Trajkovic said in his statement but from what I see here, I concluded it was the MUP staff in Pristina was asked about this, that they informed the chief that the decision had already been made earlier about the formation of this reserve force. And it says here that on the 26th of April, 1999, these reservists came to the area of deployment and were placed under our command and were involved and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Sir, you are looking right at the document which tells you the chief of the department gave his approval, and yet you still seem to be insinuating that that was not required or done. Do you not see, sir, that the chief of the department gave his approval in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying with whom my commander contacted. I really don't know who he contacted on this issue. I know that the reserve force of the MUP is handled by the Ministry of the Interior, and this is handled by the police administration. That's what the police administration sent us. I don't know anything about what Trajkovic says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, that the highest ranking person here who gave his approval is Mr. Djordjevic? There's no mention of the minister here; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what my commander said. I'm telling you again, the decision to engage the reserve force was made by the minister. My commander made contacts and implemented this through the police administration which attached to us these reservists, and it's possible that he also of informed the chief of the department, but I really don't know why he gave such notification because the chief of the department did not engage 108 members. It's the police administration who does that pursuant to the decision of the minister of the interior and sends these men to specific units. In this case they sent them to us in Prolom Banja. In fact, this was their second engagement, and the area is Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we have your position on that, sir. Sir, after this redeployment, you went out into the field along with these Skorpions or MUP reservists. Can you tell us, sir, once they joined your unit, where you were in action in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that meeting where Commander Trajkovic divided up the personnel at our command in Kosovo Polje, they were divided up between our units and we were working in the area of Jezerske mountains. I don't know if you know where Jezerske mountains are. It's in the territory close to Mount Sur [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And, sir, when you were in the field and specifically when these men were in the field with you, you would need to be able to explain to the other forces who were around and operating with you who had authorised these men to be out in the field; correct? These were not SAJ members but they were fighting with you, these were, as you say, MUP reservists. You would need to explain to other people who these men were and who had authorised them to be there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said they were attached to our unit for the purposes of that task. The decision to attach them was made by Commander Trajkovic, he guaranteed for them, that they would be working very professionally, and I never doubted for a moment, nor did my police officers with whom I worked doubt for any moment that they would be working very professionally, very honestly in the task given them in this action in which they were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we know Commander Trajkovic didn't have the authority to integrate these men into his own unit so what I'm asking you is, when you were encountering other men in the field, other Serb forces, whose authority did you tell them that these men were there on? Who had authorised these men to be out fighting in the field with the SAJ? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit, the Pristina SAJ worked with the reservists from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Nobody asked me about what you are asking me. I explained to my men, I would have explained, if they had asked me, but they didn't ask me, and it's simply because there was no need for us to have any doubts about our commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see P1595, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report to the 3rd Army Command from the field, it's actually the supplement to a report. You'll see that it's conveying information about what the Skorpions are doing in Kosovo, what this MUP reserve unit is doing in Kosovo. You can see that the first paragraph contains information about a group being warned in person in Prolom Banja; do you see that? Very first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I want to take you specifically to the third paragraph. I'll read it, sir. It says: "We also have verified information that Major-General Milan Djakovic, operative officer in the command of the 3rd Army, recognised in this group a certain Slobodan Medic, aka Boca, and asked him what sort of task had brought him there, to which the other replied that he had come by order of the MUP General Rodja." Who is MUP General Rodja, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who General Rodja was. I only knew General Vlastimir Djordjevic. As an officer who has finished military academy, I always abided by the hierarchy, and I only knew General Vlastimir Djordjevic. I don't know who this General Rodja was and what Boca was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we can safely assume for our purposes here, sir, I'll ask you to assume for our purposes here, that that is referring to General Djordjevic. We've heard a fair amount of evidence that that was his nickname. Sir, it would seem here that the explanation was being given in the field when people were asking, well, what are these men doing fighting with the MUP, it was being said, well, General Djordjevic authorised it. Can you explain, sir, why people would be saying that? Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they were saying those things. I don't know about Rodja. Frankly speaking, I don't know any Rodja who could have said these things to Boca. Boca should have received orders and should have been sent to carry out tasks by the Ministry of the Interior who was recruiting reservists, and I really don't know what he meant by saying that it was done on orders by the MUP General Rodja. I really don't know anything about what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I see my friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an answer was given, but to surmise that the witness knows anything about someone that he has never heard of in a document that was sent by a completely different service to someone else is not sufficient foundation for putting this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question was put on the basis that the witness should assume the identity, and on that assumption he has dealt with it. Whether that assumption is correct or not is a matter for other evidence, which we will have to consider in due course. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So, sir, just to put that back to you, the assumption here -- in fact, it's not an assumption, it's being stated here that it was the order of this MUP general, who I say to you is Mr. Djordjevic, he is the one who authorised these MUP reservists, these Skorpions, to be in the field. Was that not also your understanding, sir? Was that not also your knowledge of on whose authority these men were with your SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV STALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engagement of the reserve forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia is not being done based on authority. As I said before, it is done by the MUP pursuant to the decision of the minister of the interior. As I said before, the minister implements these decisions through the ministry administration, relevant administration, and it results in their admission. So there was no authority required for admission. You only need the minister's decision to admit men into the reserve forces, you don't need anyone's authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. Those are my questions for the witness. I would like to briefly address the exhibits that we discussed yesterday that I'm seeking to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: The first is 06117, and I am seeking to tender three statements as part of that package. They are actually under separate subnumbers. The first is a statement of Mr. Stalevic. The second is the statement of Dragan Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You need to give the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
